name: poplar-trie
baseline: std::unordered_map (also tsl::robin_map, tsl::htrie_map, google::dense_hash_map, cedar, libart, JudySL)
workload: Insert and lookup of string keys (14.1M English Wikipedia titles; 39.5M .uk URLs) into dynamic string-to-value maps; max resident set size, insert us/key, lookup us/key.
claimed_speedup: Memory only: compact_bonsai_map 0.24 GiB vs std::unordered_map 1.29 GiB on Wikipedia titles (about 5.4x smaller, derived from page data); 1.09 GiB vs 6.05 GiB on .uk URLs (about 5.5x smaller, derived from page data). It is slower: lookup 1.02 us/key vs 0.27 for std::unordered_map (titles), 1.44 vs 0.50 (URLs); insert 1.71 vs 0.50 us/key (titles).
hardware: One core of quad-core Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 2.80 GHz, 256 GB RAM, CentOS 6.10
tradeoffs: Compact dynamic path-decomposed trie; no deletion; several-fold slower lookups and inserts than robin_map/unordered_map; C++17.
caveats: Space win only, not a speed win. libstdc++ inferred from g++ on Linux (not stated). Benchmark driver code is in the separate repo kampersanda/dictionary_bench (not opened). Numbers are from 2018-2019 on an old Xeon.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'c-trie++ OR bST OR wavelet matrix github kampersanda C++ faster than SDSL benchmark' surfaced kampersanda's projects page; README opened on github.com

name: marisa-trie (libmarisa)
baseline: darts-clone (compacted double-array trie) and tx-trie (LOUDS-based trie)
workload: Dictionary size for 9,805,576 English Wikipedia page titles (Nov 2012, 200,435,403 bytes plain).
claimed_speedup: Size: marisa-trie 50,753,560 bytes vs tx-trie 127,727,058 vs darts-clone 376,613,888 (about 2.5x smaller than tx-trie and 7.4x smaller than darts-clone, derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 633 stars; widely used via Python marisa-trie bindings
tradeoffs: Static, read-only dictionary (LOUDS-encoded nested Patricia trie); build is slow relative to double-array tries; lookups slower than darts-clone (not measured in README).
caveats: README table reports size only; no speed numbers, compiler or hardware. Latest commit seen is a dependabot bump, so code itself is stable/finished. The marisa-trie readthedocs benchmark page was in search results but not opened (readthedocs blocked).
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'succinct trie LOUDS dictionary blog faster than marisa-trie benchmark'; README opened via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Clustered Elias-Fano Indexes (CPEF)
baseline: Partitioned Elias-Fano (PEF) and Binary Interpolative Coding (BIC) inverted index compression
workload: Space of inverted index posting lists on a Gov2 sample, bits per posting.
claimed_speedup: CPEF 4.23 bits per posting vs PEF 5.15 (+17.86%) and BIC 4.60 (+8.04%). Space only.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 5.4.1, CMake Release (flags in CMakeLists.txt not opened)
tradeoffs: Needs clustering step and Boost; built on ds2i with submodules (FastPFor, stxxl, succinct); query-time cost versus PEF is in the paper, not the README.
caveats: No LICENSE file visible (README copyright notice only), so usability is reference. README numbers are on a sample dataset in the repo, not the full Gov2/ClueWeb of the paper. Peer review is ACM TOIS 2017 (paper itself not opened; blocked). Space win, not speed.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Elias-Fano partitioned index blog benchmark faster than compressed posting lists open source C++'

name: Generalized Elias-Fano (GEF)
baseline: ALP, LeCo, DAC (random-access integer compressors); also compared with Xz and Brotli
workload: Compressed storage of arbitrary (non-monotone) integer sequences with constant-time random access, plus >1 GB/s throughput.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: up to 42.83% more compact among compressors with high throughput and random access (e.g. ALP, LeCo, DAC); matches Xz and Brotli in space while orders of magnitude faster.
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++20; generalizes Elias-Fano to unsorted sequences; repo has a benchmarks directory, benchmark_results folder and run_benchmarks.sh (contents not opened).
caveats: Numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of the project site gef.di.unipi.it (blocked, not opened); README has no numbers. Baselines are not SDSL or sux; entry is borderline for this category. Verifier should open benchmarks/ and benchmark_results/ in the repo.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Generalized Elias-Fano GEF github C++ faster than Elias-Fano partitioned compression sorted integers' (project page snippet); repo page opened on github.com
